The patient is presenting with "second sight," a phenomenon where a patient with presbyopia (age-related loss of lens elasticity) suddenly experiences an improvement in near vision. In a patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus, this is typically caused by the development of **diabetic cataracts**. 

The high glucose levels in the lens lead to the accumulation of sorbitol (via the polyol pathway), which causes osmotic swelling of the lens. This swelling increases the curvature of the lens, increasing its refractive power and shifting the focal point forward. This effectively compensates for presbyopia, allowing the patient to see near objects more clearly without glasses. This process involves the osmotic changes and denaturation/modification of lens proteins.

During pregnancy, systemic vascular resistance (SVR) decreases significantly due to the vasodilatory effects of progesterone and the development of the low-resistance uteroplacental circulation. A decrease in SVR reduces the afterload of the left ventricle, which in turn decreases the pressure in the left atrium. This creates a larger pressure gradient between the left atrium and the right atrium, thereby increasing the volume of the left-to-right shunt. This increased shunt leads to greater right ventricular volume overload, exacerbating the symptoms of dyspnea and cyanosis (due to potential paradoxical embolism or worsening right heart failure/congestion).

In elderly patients, cSDH often presents insidiously with cognitive decline (mimicking dementia) and gait disturbances. The presence of a focal deficit (decreased strength in the left lower extremity and a positive Babinski sign) suggests a mass effect on the brain.
